biggest_risk: The self-funded years between your retirement and the start of government benefits would draw heavily on your portfolio while it is still doing its heaviest lifting, concentrating sequence-of-returns pressure into a single early window.
best_lever: Extending your working years carries the most weight of any move in your file, lifting both the odds the plan holds and the wealth left at the end far more than the savings or claiming-timing alternatives.
snapshot_intro: A C+ grade reflects a plan that holds in a majority of tested paths but stumbles in a meaningful minority, leaving real room to firm up the outcome. This result reflects thousands of tested scenarios, including severe crashes and prolonged inflation, but it cannot capture every possible risk such as legislative changes, major health issues, or divorce. The starting point matters most, and you begin from a position of momentum rather than recovery.
mirror_block: You and your partner are about a decade from retiring together, and you have built a sizeable mix of registered savings, a tax-free account, non-registered money, a home, and two income properties along the way. Most of your retirement income would have to come from these assets, since government benefits would cover only a minority of your target spending. The pressure point is the stretch of self-funded years before those benefits begin, when the portfolio carries almost the whole load on its own.
revenue_analysis: The income you would aim to replace sits below your current household earnings, which softens the strain of stepping out of work and leaves the plan less reliant on everything going right. Because the bulk of that replacement income would be drawn from your own assets rather than guaranteed sources, lifestyle continuity would lean on how the portfolio behaves in the early years. A replacement level set short of full pre-retirement income gives the structure breathing room to absorb a weak stretch without forcing an abrupt change in how you live.
savings_analysis: Your savings would keep building between now and retirement, carried by steady contributions layered on top of a base that already compounds, and that combination is the main engine behind the projected capital at retirement. The trajectory rests far more on letting the existing balance grow undisturbed than on the new money you add each month, since time in the market does the heavier lifting from here. The key takeaway is momentum: the plan is accumulating, not recovering, and the runway ahead is its greatest asset.
gov_explanation: Guaranteed government income would form a dependable floor beneath your retirement, but it covers only a minority of the household spending target, so the portfolio carries the larger share for life. That floor also arrives in two distinct phases: the early self-funded years before benefits begin, when your assets stand almost alone, and the later steady state once both partners' benefits are flowing. The lighter the guaranteed floor, the more the plan's durability rests on portfolio behaviour rather than on indexed public income.
longevity_analysis: The middle band of outcomes stretches from a cautious lower end to a far higher favourable end, and half of all tested paths land somewhere inside that range. The width of that band reflects how much rests on returns and the order in which they arrive during your early retirement years. The cautious edge is not a worst case but a sober reminder that a weak start would leave you with materially less room than the median path suggests.
what_if_analysis: Of the alternatives tested, working longer moves the odds the most, lifting both the chance the plan holds and the wealth that survives by a wide margin over saving more or shifting when benefits start. That sensitivity reveals where the plan is most exposed: its outcome turns less on contribution size than on how many years the portfolio works before it must start paying out and absorbing early-retirement sequence risk.
strategy_comparison: Against the status-quo path, working longer stands clearly apart, lifting the odds the plan holds from sound toward solid and adding the largest gain in surviving wealth of any option modeled. The saving-more and early registered drawdown paths each nudge the result upward only slightly, and delaying the Canada Pension Plan claim trades a touch of success odds for added longevity protection, so the standout lever is time worked rather than any single financial tweak.
priority_actions: What governs your outcome more than anything is the size of your planned spending set against income that would lean heavily on the portfolio rather than on guaranteed benefits. Pulled against assets in the early self-funded years, that target translates into a withdrawal pace the portfolio can sustain in most paths but not all, which is exactly what holds the grade where it sits. Trimming the early draw, even by a manageable monthly amount, could buy the plan years of added autonomy. With a decade still to run and savings already flowing, the trajectory you are on could carry the plan from sound toward solid well before you retire.
tax_analysis: Your effective tax rate today and the rate you would face in retirement sit at similar levels, which means there is no large bracket arbitrage waiting to be captured by simply shifting income across the line. The leverage instead lies in the order accounts are drawn down and in coordinating taxable income across both partners.
fees_analysis: Your investment fees run at a notably light rate for an unspecified vehicle, and over the full life of the plan the cumulative drag would amount to only a small fraction of retirement income, costing the plan just a sliver of a single year's spending. That is a structural strength rather than a leak, leaving the heavy levers in spending pace and years worked rather than in cost.
couple_analysis: As a couple retiring in step, the leverage sits in coordinating which accounts each of you draws from first, so taxable income stays spread across both hands rather than bunched in one bracket, and in leaning on survivor benefits that would carry forward. If the primary earner were to die first, the surviving partner would keep their own benefits, gain a survivor pension top-up, and receive the tax-free account intact, though household income would step down and reshape the draw. If the partner were to die first, the registered accounts would consolidate with the primary, shifting the tax exposure the other way; the partner's own accumulated savings make either trajectory less fragile than a single-earner plan would be.
property_analysis: Your home carries a remaining mortgage against a substantial value, and alongside two income properties it places a large share of household wealth in real estate. Because no sale is scheduled, the projection treats none of this equity as spendable retirement income, so it stands in reserve: a concentrated, illiquid backstop that could be tapped through a future decision but plays no active role in funding the draw as modeled.
estate_analysis: The median path would leave a substantial estate, while the cautious tail shows that a weak sequence could consume it entirely, and that spread is the honest centre of the picture. With a balanced preference between spending freely and leaving a legacy, the plan already threads both aims without forcing a choice. The size of that potential estate is a by-product of a portfolio kept working, not a target you set, so it would flex with how the early years unfold.
obs_1: **Bridge funding load**: The self-funded years before government benefits begin would demand a large cumulative draw from your portfolio precisely when it is largest and most exposed, compressing your single greatest source of sequence risk into one early window rather than spreading it across retirement.
obs_2: **Rental income role**: Your two income properties produce a pre-tax rental stream, net of modeled expenses, that would arrive independently of market returns and ease the draw your portfolio has to carry, though it is rental income rather than guaranteed net cash flow and would move with vacancy, upkeep, and rate cycles.
obs_3: **Illiquid weight**: Your home and income properties tie up a large share of household net worth in assets that cannot be sold a slice at a time, so this wealth stands in reserve rather than as spendable retirement income, and the projection draws nothing from your home equity.
obs_4: **Two-phase floor**: Once both partners' benefits are flowing in the steady-state years, guaranteed government income would cover only a minority of the household spending target, and the earlier self-funded years carry little of that floor at all, so the two phases ask very different things of your portfolio rather than imposing a single constant load.
obs_5: **Effort meets ceiling**: Your saving discipline already runs at a strong pace, yet the plan's odds sit only at a sound level, which points to the limiting factor being not how much you set aside but the spending target and the early-draw pressure it creates against a lightly supported portfolio.
next_horizon: The data suggests the years still ahead of retirement could be the highest-leverage window for firming up the plan, since adjustments to spending intent or draw sequencing made now would compound across the longest runway you have left. The next update of this assessment, in a year, would measure how the trajectory has moved against the path shown here.
model_blind_spots: The projection cannot fully capture pension income splitting between you and your partner, which could meaningfully lower the household tax load once income flows from registered accounts. Nor does it weigh a future sale of your home or income properties, any one of which could reshape the asset picture and the early-draw pressure. The precise tax and vacancy behaviour of the rental income is modeled only at a net level, and career shifts, an inheritance, or a separation would each bend the plan in ways no single run can foresee. These dimensions could be explored in a future review.
